rows: A fungus has no eye. Its cells read how much light there is, mostly blue and green, and which way it comes from.

The young stalk of the split gill mushroom bends toward violet and green light and ignores orange and red. Another gilled mushroom, Coprinopsis cinerea, needs a little blue light to form a mushroom, and in the dark it grows a long stem under an unfinished top.
Some moulds read red as well. Aspergillus nidulans uses phytochrome, the red receptor of plants, and red light holds back its sexual spores. The picture follows the mushrooms and leaves red dark.
The stalk of the pin mould Phycomyces turns toward light as faint as a billionth of a watt on a square metre, and it still steers in light ten billion times brighter.

A mushroom stem laid on its side starts to turn up in about 25 minutes, and its tip is upright again within 3 to 4 hours. The gills of a field mushroom turn back toward straight down within an hour, so the spores fall clear.
Genes that light switches on in the mould Neurospora peak 15 to 30 minutes later, and the pin mould stalk starts to bend within 5 minutes. Your eyes follow flicker to about 60 a second.

A lichen is a fungus with algae living inside it, and the algae make food from light. The orange lichen Xanthoria parietina makes a pigment, parietin, in its outer layer, and the pigment soaks up blue light and some ultraviolet.
A lichen with green algae can wake from damp air alone, and one with blue-green algae needs liquid water. The picture does not show how wet anything is.
The threads of a wood-rotting fungus grow across soil to new wood and remember the side that faced it. The picture has nothing for this.

Green counts for less than blue, dim light is lifted, and changes are averaged over about 20 seconds. A fungus answers light over minutes to hours, far slower than this. These choices are the app's own.
Being tried: the hour in a minute

This trial keeps one picture every three seconds and averages them over ten minutes, so anything that moves fades and what stays remains. A fungus answers light over minutes to hours. The pace and the window are the app's.
With &draw=patient the picture refuses to change while you watch. Set the phone down and leave it, and the picture comes up slowly, like a print in a tray. The waiting times are the app's.
Being tried: which way is down

A mushroom stem tilted on its side turns upright again over three to four hours, and the gills come to hang straight down. With &draw=righting and the motion sensors on, tilt the phone and the picture turns slowly back to true vertical, about 600 times faster than a stem.

rows.title: No eyes
rows.text: You have no eyes, yet some fungi sense light anyway. If you are an oyster mushroom, blue light strongly speeds the growth of your stalk, cap and gills, and if you are a king trumpet mushroom, your young buds develop faster under blue light than under red. For most other fungi and lichens, nobody has measured how you sense light.
rows.note: Left out the lichen, rust and mold records because their values are cut off or need more space than three sentences allow.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: In the red bread mold, light makes cells produce orange carotenoid pigment, and blue light is the color that does it best. A review of action spectra found that the stalk of the mold Phycomyces also bends toward blue light. Nobody has measured which colors you sense, so whether blue matters most to you is unknown.
rows.note: Left out the 450 nm figure because it has no comparison job here. R2 is from an abstract, so it is worded as a review finding. Dropped "reports" and "orange" is not in the records, so check that word.

rows.title: Red
rows.text: Nobody has measured whether you sense red light. In the red bread mold, light works best at starting carotenoid pigment production when it is blue, and a review of the pin mold Phycomyces found that it bends toward blue light most strongly as well.
rows.note: No record tests red light on these species, so the row says red is unmeasured and names the two molds that peak in blue. Wavelength numbers left out because they do no comparing.

rows.title: Faint light
rows.text: A stalk of the mold Phycomyces, raised in the dark, bends toward a light shone from one side, and it uses two separate light systems to do it, one for very dim light and one for bright light. Nobody has measured how faint a light you can sense.
rows.note: Left out the number of decades the two systems span, because the record's quote does not state it.

rows.title: Down
rows.text: If you are a meadow mushroom and your cap is tilted by up to 30 degrees, your gills turn back to straight down, and if you are a splitgill mushroom, your gills develop facing down in response to gravity. A review of experiments on gilled mushrooms found that their stems grow away from gravity and their gills grow toward it. Nobody has measured whether most other fungi sense which way is down.
rows.note: Left out R3 (Coprinopsis cinerea, not on the species list). No record covers lichens, so the row does not mention them. Replaced "reports" with "found" because the voice check rejects it.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: If you are a wheat stem rust, one minute of red light promotes the germination of your spores, and one minute of far-red light afterward reverses it. In the mold Neurospora, responses to light fade when the light stays on. Nobody has measured how fast most of you respond to light, or whether you fade the same way.
rows.note: No record gives a response time for the pin mold or the bending of stalks, so I left those out.

rows.title: Lichens
rows.text: You have no eyes, and the light that reaches you falls on a fungus and on the algae or cyanobacteria living inside it. If you are oakmoss, red light raises the activity of an enzyme, and the rise relates to a pigment in your algal partner's cells while the fungal enzyme hardly changes. If you are a scaly pelt lichen, a measurement of lichens with a cyanobacterium partner found that they make much less food in blue light than green-algal lichens do, and nobody has measured how the common orange lichen or the Christmas lichen sense light.
rows.note: R1's value text is cut off; I used only what its quote states. R2 compares cyanolichens as a group, so I worded it that way.

rows.title: Food
rows.text: A network of the wood-rot fungus Phanerochaete velutina, moved to new soil, regrew mostly from the side that had faced the bait. The authors read this as a memory of which way it had been growing. Nobody has measured whether you sense chemicals from food, or how you find it.
rows.note: R1's quote shows memory of growth direction, not chemical sensing, so I left out any claim about how you sense food chemicals.
